The glory that the second temple lacked came in the person of Jesus, who walked in its courts and called his body the true temple. Believers are being built into that greater house. The promise of 'peace in this place' is the peace Christ gives (Ephesians 2:14-17).

Dispensationalists (Feinberg, Walvoord, Fruchtenbaum) note that Haggai treats the temple on the site as one house through its history ('this house in its former glory', Haggai 2:3). The shaking of the heavens and the overthrow of the thrones of kingdoms (Haggai 2:21-22) have not yet happened in full, so the 'latter glory' will be seen in the millennial temple when Messiah returns to Jerusalem. Christ's visits to Herod's temple were a foretaste, not the fulfilment.

Fulfilment writers (Beale, Baldwin, Robertson) answer that Hebrews 12:26-28 interprets Haggai's shaking as the passing of the old order and the giving of an unshakable kingdom, which believers are receiving now. The glory came when God's Son, the true dwelling of God (John 1:14), entered the very temple Haggai spoke to, before it was destroyed in AD 70. A later building on the same site could not be 'this house' in a stronger sense than the house Jesus himself entered.

Future-camp writers reply that Hebrews 12:27 places the removal of shaken things in the future ('yet once more'), so the shaking is not finished. Haggai's promise of peace 'in this place' was not seen when Jesus came, because the same temple was destroyed by Rome within forty years. They therefore expect a final fulfilment at Jerusalem.
The Branch will build the temple and sit as priest on his throne

Zechariah is told to make crowns and set one on the head of Joshua the high priest, and to say: here is the man whose name is the Branch. He will branch out from his place and build the temple of the LORD. He will bear royal honour and sit and rule on his throne, and he will be a priest on his throne, with peace between the two offices. Those who are far off will come and help build the temple (Zechariah 6:15).
The Branch will build the LORD's temple and be both king and priest on one throne.
The hands of Zerubbabel, of David's line, laid the foundation of the house and will finish it. He and Joshua the priest are signs of the coming Branch.
Jesus claims he will raise the temple in three days; John explains that he means his own body, raised from the dead.
Believers have a high priest who sits at the right hand of the throne of the Majesty in heaven, a minister in the true tent that the Lord set up.
Those once 'far off' are brought near by Christ's blood. With the apostles and prophets as foundation and Christ as cornerstone, they grow into a holy temple in the Lord.
The one who conquers will be made a pillar in the temple of God and will bear the name of the city of God, the new Jerusalem.

Zechariah's night visions are dated to the twenty-fourth day of the eleventh month in the second year of Darius I, about February 519 BC (Zechariah 1:7), during the rebuilding of the second temple. Zerubbabel, grandson of King Jehoiachin (1 Chronicles 3:17-19), led the builders, yet the crown in Zechariah 6:11 is set on Joshua the high priest. Under the Mosaic order king and priest were separate offices, and King Uzziah was struck with leprosy for burning incense (2 Chronicles 26:16-21). Zechariah's picture of a priest-king is therefore remarkable. The Qumran community expected two messiahs, one priestly and one royal (1QS IX 11), which shows how unusual it was to unite them.

Jesus is both the King who rules his people and the Priest who reconciles them to God. He is building his temple now from people far and near, and every believer is a living stone in it (1 Peter 2:4-5). Because he is both, there is 'peace' between God's rule and God's mercy in his work.

Dispensationalists (Walvoord, Feinberg, Fruchtenbaum) agree that the Branch is the Messiah, but argue that 'he shall build the temple' refers to the millennial temple of Ezekiel 40-48, which he will build after his return. They connect Zechariah 6 with Zechariah 14:16-21, where the surviving nations go up to Jerusalem year by year to worship the King and keep the Feast of Booths. This, they say, describes literal worship in Jerusalem after Christ returns.

Fulfilment writers (Beale, Robertson, Baldwin) answer that Jesus himself applies the temple-building role to his resurrection (John 2:19-21), and that the New Testament repeatedly calls the church, gathered around the risen Christ, God's temple (1 Corinthians 3:16; Ephesians 2:21; 1 Peter 2:5). The note that 'those far off' will help to build (Zechariah 6:15) matches Paul's language for Gentiles brought near (Ephesians 2:13, 17). Christ already sits as priest on his throne (Hebrews 8:1; Psalms 110:4), so the union of offices that Zechariah foresaw has happened.

Dispensationalists reply that Zechariah 14 includes features that are hard to read spiritually: the Mount of Olives split in two (Zechariah 14:4), punishment by drought on nations that do not come up to Jerusalem (14:17-19), and the Feast of Booths kept by Egypt. They argue this requires an earthly kingdom with Jerusalem as its centre.
Return after seventy years

Jeremiah wrote to the exiles in Babylon that when seventy years were complete for Babylon, the LORD would visit them and bring them back to Jerusalem. The same letter tells them to build houses, seek the welfare of the city of their exile, and pray for it (Jeremiah 29:5-7). The seventy years are also announced in Jeremiah 25:11-12.
God fixes a limit to the exile: seventy years for Babylon, then a visit of grace and a return to 'this place'.

In the first year of Cyrus king of Persia (538 BC) the LORD stirs Cyrus to issue a decree: the God of heaven has charged him to build a house in Jerusalem, and any of His people may go up. The writer says this happened 'that the word of the LORD by the mouth of Jeremiah might be fulfilled'.

Daniel reads Jeremiah's seventy years in the first year of Darius the Mede and prays for the city. Gabriel answers with a longer horizon of 'seventy sevens' (Daniel 9:24), so the return from Babylon becomes a pointer to a greater release.
Matthew structures Jesus' genealogy around 'the deportation to Babylon' and 'the Christ'. The exile only truly ends when the Son of David comes to save his people from their sins (Matthew 1:21).
Peter addresses believers in Asia Minor as 'elect exiles of the dispersion'. The church lives as a people in exile, seeking the good of the city where it lives, as Jeremiah's letter instructed.
The voice from heaven calls, 'Come out of her, my people', as Babylon falls. The final exodus from 'Babylon' ends all exile in the new Jerusalem.

Jerusalem fell to Nebuchadnezzar in 587/586 BC after earlier deportations in 605 and 597 BC. Babylon fell to Cyrus in 539 BC, and the Cyrus Cylinder (British Museum) records his policy of returning displaced peoples and their gods to their sanctuaries, which matches the setting of Ezra 1. About 42,360 people returned with Zerubbabel and Jeshua (Ezra 2:64), the second temple was finished in the sixth year of Darius I, about 516/515 BC (Ezra 6:15), and Ezra (458/457 BC) and Nehemiah (445/444 BC) followed. Many Jews chose to stay in Babylon, Persia and Egypt, so the Second Temple period had both a restored community in Judea and a wide diaspora.

The fulfilment reading holds that the return from Babylon proved God keeps his word to the day, but it also left Israel under foreign rule, still waiting for the full end of exile (Nehemiah 9:36-37). That greater return comes through Christ, who forgives the sins that caused exile. Christians are told to live like Jeremiah's exiles: settle, work, pray for the city, and wait for the homecoming (Hebrews 13:14).

Dispensationalists fully agree that Jeremiah 29:10 was fulfilled literally in 538 BC, and they see this as the model for reading all the return promises. Because God kept the seventy years literally and in the land, they argue, the later promises of a final and permanent return (Jeremiah 30-33; Amos 9:15, 'they shall no more be pulled up') must also be literal and are not yet exhausted. The Babylonian return was partial and temporary; the land was lost again in AD 70 and AD 135, so a final regathering remains.

The fulfilment reading agrees that the return was literal and argues that the New Testament itself presents the deeper, unfinished part of the hope as met in Jesus (Luke 1:68-79; Luke 2:25, 'the consolation of Israel'). The prophets tied the permanent return to a new covenant, a new heart and a Davidic king; these the New Testament says have come (Luke 22:20; Acts 2:30-36). So the literal pattern is real, but its final form is the resurrection people in a renewed creation, not a second political return.

Dispensationalists answer that the fulfilment reading accepts a literal first stage and then changes method for the second. If the seventy years were exact and geographic, consistency suggests the 'no more pulled up' promise (Amos 9:15) will also be geographic. Progressive dispensationalists add that the land can be included in the new creation without being spiritualised away.
Regathering from all the nations

Moses foresees Israel scattered among all the nations for covenant unfaithfulness. When they return to the LORD with all their heart, he will gather them even from 'the outermost parts of heaven' and bring them into the land (Deuteronomy 30:1-5), and he will circumcise their heart (30:6). Isaiah 11:11-12 speaks of the Lord recovering his remnant 'a second time' from Assyria, Egypt, Cush, Elam and the coastlands, and Jeremiah 16:14-15 says this gathering will eclipse the exodus from Egypt.
The gathering follows repentance: the LORD will restore their fortunes and gather them from all the peoples.
The returning assembly of 42,360 under Cyrus is a first, partial gathering, but many tribes and families remain scattered.
The 'root of Jesse' stands as a signal for the peoples, and the nations seek him; Paul quotes this of Christ's ministry to Gentiles in Romans 15:12.
John explains that Jesus would die not for the nation only, but to gather into one the children of God scattered abroad.
At Pentecost, devout Jews 'from every nation under heaven' are gathered in Jerusalem and hear the gospel, and about 3,000 are baptised (Acts 2:41).
The Son of Man sends his angels to gather his elect from the four winds, the final regathering.

By the first century the Jewish diaspora was larger than the population of Judea: there were large communities in Babylonia, Alexandria in Egypt, Syria, Asia Minor and Rome. Luke's list in Acts 2:9-11 (Parthians, Medes, Elamites, Mesopotamia, Judea, Cappadocia, Pontus, Asia, Phrygia, Pamphylia, Egypt, Libya near Cyrene, Rome, Crete and Arabia) reads like a map of that diaspora, and it overlaps strikingly with the lands named in Isaiah 11:11. Pilgrims came to Jerusalem for the great feasts, so Pentecost brought the scattered people to Zion.

On the fulfilment reading, the regathering is completed as Jesus gathers the scattered people of God, Jew first and then Gentile, into one flock around himself. Deuteronomy 30:6 (a circumcised heart) is the inner condition, and Paul applies heart circumcision to all believers (Romans 2:28-29; Colossians 2:11). Believers today are part of the gathering, and they join in it by mission to every nation.

Dispensational writers such as Walvoord and Fruchtenbaum argue that Isaiah 11:11 speaks of a 'second' worldwide regathering, the first being from Babylon, and that the return of Jews since the late nineteenth century and the founding of the State of Israel in 1948 begin it. Fruchtenbaum distinguishes a regathering in unbelief, in preparation for judgment (Ezekiel 20:33-38; Zephaniah 2:1-2), from a final regathering in faith after Messiah returns. They note that the promise is to the land given to the fathers (Deuteronomy 30:5), which a spiritual reading cannot satisfy.

Fulfilment writers reply that Isaiah 11:16 explains 'second time' by comparison with the exodus from Egypt, so the first gathering is the exodus and the second is the post-exilic and messianic gathering, not a twentieth-century event. Deuteronomy 30:1-2 places the return after heartfelt return to the LORD, while the founding of the modern state was led mainly by a secular national movement. The New Testament applies the gathering language to Jesus' mission (John 11:52) and to Pentecost, and does not point to a later political return.

Dispensationalists answer that Ezekiel 36:24-27 and 37:7-10 put the physical gathering before the cleansing and the giving of the Spirit, so a return in unbelief fits the order. They argue that John 11:52 adds the Gentiles without cancelling the land promise, and that Jesus himself spoke of Jerusalem being trampled 'until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled' (Luke 21:24), which implies a change for Jerusalem afterwards.
The valley of dry bones and the two sticks

Ezekiel sees a valley of very dry bones. At the prophetic word they come together and are covered with flesh, and then breath (ruach) enters them and they stand as a great army (Ezekiel 37:7-10). God explains that the bones are 'the whole house of Israel', who say 'our hope is lost', and promises to open their graves, put his Spirit in them and bring them into the land (37:11-14). The sign of the two sticks follows: Judah and Joseph (Ephraim) will become one nation under one king, 'David my servant', one shepherd, with an everlasting covenant of peace and God's sanctuary among them for ever (37:15-28).
God promises to open the graves of his people and bring them into the land of Israel, so that they know he is the LORD.

At the dedication of the second temple the returned exiles offer twelve male goats 'according to the number of the tribes of Israel'. The small community sees itself as all Israel restored, a first sign of the two sticks joined.

The risen Jesus breathes on his disciples and says 'Receive the Holy Spirit'. The Greek Old Testament uses the same verb (emphysao) in Ezekiel 37:9 and Genesis 2:7, so new creation life comes from the risen king.
Jesus, the good shepherd, says there will be 'one flock, one shepherd', which echoes Ezekiel 37:24 and 34:23.
Christ makes 'one new man' from Jew and Gentile and reconciles both in one body through the cross, which the fulfilment reading sees as the widest form of the two sticks becoming one.
The dwelling of God is with people; Ezekiel 37:27 ('my dwelling place shall be with them') is finally realised in the new creation, after the bodily resurrection.

Ezekiel prophesied among the deportees by the Chebar canal in Babylonia from 593 BC. The northern kingdom (Ephraim) had been taken by Assyria in 722 BC (2 Kings 17:6), and Judah's temple fell in 586 BC, so 'our bones are dried up' was the exiles' own lament. The 'ten lost tribes' were not wholly lost: people from the north joined Judah at different times (2 Chronicles 30:11; 2 Chronicles 34:9), and the New Testament mentions Anna 'of the tribe of Asher' (Luke 2:36) and 'our twelve tribes' (Acts 26:7). Second Temple Jews still longed for a full reunion and the resurrection, which Daniel 12:2 also promised.

The fulfilment reading holds that Ezekiel 37 is fulfilled in stages: the return from exile, the resurrection of Jesus and the gift of the Spirit, the new birth of believers (Ephesians 2:1-5), and the final bodily resurrection. The text shows that a people can be restored only by God's word and Spirit. Believers, Jew and Gentile, are one flock under one shepherd, and Paul quotes Ezekiel 37:27 about the church as God's temple (2 Corinthians 6:16).

Many dispensationalists see the founding of Israel in 1948 as bones coming together 'without breath' (Ezekiel 37:8): a nation formed in unbelief, awaiting the Spirit at Christ's return. They stress the concrete details: the land of Israel (37:12, 37:21), one nation on 'the mountains of Israel' (37:22), and the end of the north-south split, which they say no church-age event has satisfied. The sanctuary 'in their midst for evermore' (37:26-28) leads into the temple vision of Ezekiel 40-48, which they expect in the millennium.

Fulfilment writers answer that 37:11 explains the bones as the exiles' despair in the sixth century BC, not as a twentieth-century state, and that Paul and Jesus explicitly use the passage's covenant and shepherd language for the church (2 Corinthians 6:16; John 10:16). The text's own order is word and Spirit first, then life; a nation formed by a secular movement does not match a resurrection by the Spirit. The 'everlasting' sanctuary is the presence of God in Christ and his people (John 2:19-21), completed in Revelation 21:22.

Dispensationalists reply that Ezekiel 37:7-8 shows two stages, bones assembled and then breath, so a gathering before spiritual life is in the text. They hold that the church's share in the blessings of the new covenant does not exhaust the specific promise of one nation in the land under the Davidic king, and they point to Romans 11:26-27 as a future national conversion that would complete the picture.

The LORD promises a new covenant with the house of Israel and the house of Judah, not like the covenant broken after the exodus. He will put his law within them and write it on their hearts; all will know him, from least to greatest; and he will forgive their iniquity and remember their sin no more. The following verses (31:35-37) say Israel will not cease as a nation before God while sun and moon remain.
God will write his law on their hearts and be their God, and they will be his people.
Moses sprinkles 'the blood of the covenant' at Sinai, the pattern that the new covenant both echoes and surpasses.
At the Last Supper Jesus calls the cup 'the new covenant in my blood, which is poured out for you'.

Hebrews quotes Jeremiah 31:31-34 in full and says Jesus is mediator of this 'better covenant' (8:6). Hebrews 8:13 adds that the first covenant is 'becoming obsolete and growing old' and is 'ready to vanish away'.
Paul calls himself and his co-workers 'ministers of a new covenant', written by the Spirit 'on tablets of human hearts' (3:3).
Believers have come to 'Jesus, the mediator of a new covenant', within the heavenly Jerusalem that will be fully revealed at the end.

Jeremiah gave this word around the fall of Jerusalem (587/586 BC), when the Sinai covenant's curses had fallen. In the Second Temple period the Qumran community called itself the people of 'the new covenant in the land of Damascus' (Damascus Document), showing that Jews of Jesus' time longed for it. Jesus' words at the Passover meal, in Jerusalem about AD 30 or 33, claim that it is inaugurated by his death. Hebrews, written probably before AD 70 (disputed), says the old order is 'ready to vanish', and the temple and its sacrifices ended with the Roman destruction in AD 70.

On the fulfilment reading, every believer, Jew or Gentile, is already a member of the new covenant made 'with the house of Israel', because they are in Christ, the true Israel. This is why the Lord's Supper is called the new covenant (1 Corinthians 11:25), and why Christians have full forgiveness, the indwelling Spirit and direct knowledge of God. The covenant's promises are the believer's present inheritance, not a later Jewish dispensation.

Dispensationalists stress that Jeremiah names the parties: the house of Israel and the house of Judah, and they link it to Israel's continuing national existence in 31:35-37. Classic dispensationalists held various views (Chafer once proposed two new covenants; Ryrie and Walvoord teach one covenant whose spiritual blessings the church shares now while its national and land aspects await Israel). Progressive dispensationalists such as Blaising, Bock and Saucy say the covenant is inaugurated at the cross but will be fully realised when 'all Israel' is saved (Romans 11:26-27 quotes Isaiah 59:21 and Jeremiah 31:34).

Fulfilment writers answer that Hebrews applies the very text, including 'house of Israel', to its Christian readers without any hint of a later second stage for the nation. Since Gentiles are grafted into Israel's olive tree (Romans 11:17), the covenant with 'Israel' includes them. Jeremiah 31:35-37 is fulfilled in the continuing existence of Israel as the remnant and the Messiah's people, who will never cease (Matthew 16:18).

Dispensationalists answer that Hebrews 8 shows the covenant has begun, not that Israel's national role is ended. Romans 11:27 places the covenant's removal of Israel's sins in connection with a future saving of 'all Israel' after 'the fullness of the Gentiles has come in' (11:25). They hold that a covenant can be inaugurated with Gentile participants while its national promises await the nation.
A new heart and a new spirit

God will take Israel from the nations and bring them into their own land, sprinkle clean water on them and cleanse them from idols, give them a new heart and a new spirit, remove the heart of stone and give a heart of flesh, and put his Spirit within them so that they walk in his statutes (Ezekiel 36:24-27). Then they will dwell in the land and be his people (36:28). God says he acts for the sake of his holy name, which Israel had profaned among the nations (36:22).
God promises a new heart and a new spirit, replacing the heart of stone.
The returned exiles, with those who had separated themselves from the uncleanness of the nations, keep the Passover: a first, partial cleansing.
Jesus tells Nicodemus that no one enters God's kingdom unless born 'of water and the Spirit', and rebukes the 'teacher of Israel' for not knowing it (3:10), which points to Ezekiel 36:25-27.
The exalted Jesus pours out the promised Holy Spirit on Jews gathered from the nations at Pentecost.
Paul says the Corinthians are a letter of Christ written by the Spirit 'on tablets of human hearts' (literally hearts of flesh), echoing Ezekiel 36:26.
The one who overcomes will inherit all things; God will be his God and he will be God's son, the covenant formula completed.

Ezekiel spoke this after news of Jerusalem's fall reached the exiles (Ezekiel 33:21, about 585 BC). After the return, the reforms of Ezra and Nehemiah (Ezra 9-10; Nehemiah 8-10) show both a real turning to the law and repeated failure (Nehemiah 13), so the 'new heart' was still awaited. At Pentecost in Jerusalem, the Spirit came on Jews 'from every nation under heaven' (Acts 2:5), the very people taken from the nations that Ezekiel had described, and Peter then offered the Spirit to 'all who are far off' (Acts 2:39).

The fulfilment reading holds that every Christian has received what Ezekiel promised: cleansing, a new heart and the indwelling Spirit (Titus 3:5; Romans 8:9). Obedience is the fruit of this inner change, not its cause. Because Gentiles receive the same Spirit (Acts 10:44-47; Acts 15:8-9), they share in the restoration that Ezekiel promised to Israel.

Dispensationalists point to the order in Ezekiel 36:24-25: first God takes Israel from the nations into its own land, then he sprinkles clean water. They see a regathering in unbelief (beginning in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries) followed by a national new birth at Christ's return (Zechariah 12:10; Romans 11:26). The church receives the Spirit now, but the promise to the nation in its land, with 'the cities inhabited and the waste places rebuilt' (36:33-35), is still future.

Fulfilment writers answer that the New Testament places the giving of this Spirit at Pentecost, to Jews gathered in Jerusalem from the nations, so the order of Ezekiel 36 has already been enacted. The new heart cannot be given to a nation as a political unit; it is given to persons who believe, whether Jew or Gentile. The rebuilt cities and fruitful land are, in this view, fulfilled typologically after the exile and finally in the renewed earth.

Dispensationalists reply that Pentecost was a real beginning but not the national, complete renewal described: 'I will save you from all your uncleanness' (36:29) concerns 'the house of Israel' as a whole (36:22, 36:32). Paul's hope for 'all Israel' (Romans 11:26) confirms, they say, that the nation's corporate renewal is still ahead.
The Spirit poured out on all flesh

After a plague of locusts and a call to repentance, God promises that 'afterward' he will pour out his Spirit on all flesh: sons and daughters will prophesy, old men dream, young men see visions, even servants receive the Spirit. There will be wonders in heaven and earth, the sun turned to darkness and the moon to blood before the great day of the LORD, and whoever calls on the name of the LORD will be saved, with deliverance in Mount Zion and Jerusalem (Joel 2:32).
God will pour his Spirit on all flesh, without distinction of age, sex or social rank.
Moses wished that all the LORD's people were prophets and that he would put his Spirit on them; Joel promises exactly this.
John the Baptist says the coming one will baptise with the Holy Spirit and fire.
Peter says 'this is what was spoken by the prophet Joel' and quotes the whole passage, adding 'in the last days'.
Paul quotes Joel 2:32 ('everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved') and applies it to Jew and Greek alike (10:12), with 'Lord' meaning Jesus (10:9).
The Spirit and the bride say 'Come'; the Spirit-filled people call the world until the final day of the Lord.

Joel's date is disputed (proposals range from the ninth to the fourth century BC). The fulfilment happened at the feast of Weeks (Shavuot, Pentecost) in Jerusalem around AD 30 or 33, when Jewish pilgrims and proselytes from Parthia to Rome were present (Acts 2:9-11) and about 3,000 believed (Acts 2:41). Peter adds 'to all who are far off' (Acts 2:39), and the same Spirit later falls on Samaritans (Acts 8:17) and on the Gentile household of Cornelius (Acts 10:44-45). Within a generation, in AD 70, Jerusalem itself fell, which many fulfilment writers connect with the 'great and awesome day' that Peter warned about (Acts 2:40, 'this crooked generation').

On the fulfilment reading, the church lives in Joel's 'last days': every believer has the Spirit and shares the prophetic calling to speak of God's works. The 'all flesh' of Joel is shown to include the Gentiles. The promise of rescue to 'whoever calls on the name of the LORD' is the basis of evangelism to every nation today.

Some dispensationalists, including Fruchtenbaum, hold that Acts 2 is an application or a partial fulfilment, because the signs of Joel 2:30-31 (blood, fire, darkened sun, blood-red moon) did not occur visibly at Pentecost. They note that Joel's context is Israel's land and harvest restored (2:18-27) and the nations judged in the valley of Jehoshaphat (Joel 3), which they place at the end of the tribulation. Progressive dispensationalists, such as Bock, accept a real initial fulfilment at Pentecost while expecting the cosmic signs and full national blessing at Christ's return.

Fulfilment writers note that Peter does not say 'this is like' but 'this is what was spoken' (Acts 2:16) and quotes the signs too. Cosmic darkening is a standard prophetic image for the fall of a power (Isaiah 13:10 for Babylon; Ezekiel 32:7 for Egypt), and the darkness at the crucifixion (Luke 23:44-45) and the judgment of AD 70 fit the 'day' Peter warns of. Paul's use of Joel 2:32 for Gentiles in Romans 10 shows that 'Zion' deliverance is now through faith in Jesus.

Dispensationalists answer that an 'already, not yet' fulfilment, which progressive dispensationalists accept, still leaves room for future events: the cosmic signs appear again in Jesus' teaching about his coming (Matthew 24:29) and in Revelation 6:12. They hold that Joel 3:1 ('when I restore the fortunes of Judah and Jerusalem') ties the outpouring to a national restoration that is still future.
The nations stream to Zion

In the latter days the mountain of the LORD's house will be raised above the hills, and all nations will flow to it, saying 'Let us go up to the mountain of the LORD' to learn his ways. Instruction (torah) will go out from Zion and the word of the LORD from Jerusalem; he will judge between nations, and they will beat swords into ploughshares and learn war no more. Micah 4:1-3 gives almost the same oracle.
Many peoples come to Zion to be taught, and the word of the LORD goes out from Jerusalem.
Solomon prays that foreigners who come because of God's great name will be heard when they pray toward the temple, so that all peoples may know him.
The risen Jesus says repentance and forgiveness will be proclaimed in his name to all nations, 'beginning from Jerusalem'; the word goes out from Zion.
The witnesses go from Jerusalem to Judea, Samaria and the end of the earth.
Believers 'have come to Mount Zion', the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem; the nations now come to Zion by coming to Christ.
The nations walk by the light of the new Jerusalem and the kings of the earth bring their glory into it.

Isaiah prophesied in Jerusalem in the eighth century BC, when the temple mount was small and Judah was threatened by Assyria. In the Second Temple period Herod's rebuilt temple (begun about 20/19 BC) had a large Court of the Gentiles, and many Gentile 'God-fearers' attached themselves to synagogues (Acts 10:2; Acts 13:16), while proselytes came on pilgrimage (Acts 2:10; the Ethiopian official in Acts 8:27). After Pentecost the gospel went out from Jerusalem to Samaria (Acts 8), Antioch (Acts 11:20-21) and Rome, and in AD 70 the temple itself was destroyed.

The fulfilment reading holds that Christians from the nations are the peoples who have 'gone up' to Zion, by coming to Jesus and learning his ways. The word from Zion is the gospel, and every believer joins in sending it to the nations. The beating of swords into ploughshares has begun in the reconciled community of the church (Ephesians 2:14-17) and will be complete when Christ judges the nations at the end.

Dispensationalists read this as a picture of the millennial kingdom: Christ will reign from a literal, physically exalted Jerusalem (Zechariah 14:10 speaks of the land levelled and Jerusalem raised), the nations will go up to it (Zechariah 14:16), and world disarmament will occur. They point out that universal peace has clearly not arrived in history, so the passage must refer to a future age on this earth, before the eternal state.
